headline: Fungi Finally Get a Global Conservation Plan
meta_description: At a UN biodiversity conference in Armenia, scientists from 30 countries launched the first global strategy to protect fungi—nature's overlooked ecosystem engi…
summary_short: Fungi are getting their moment. Scientists from 30 countries just launched the first-ever global conservation strategy for this vital kingdom of life.
body:
For the first time, fungi have a seat at the global conservation table. On October 21 at the United Nations biodiversity conference in Armenia, a team of mycologists from 30 countries unveiled the first comprehensive global strategy dedicated to protecting fungi. Led by Greg Mueller, chief scientist emeritus at the Chicago Botanic Garden, the initiative aims to integrate fungal conservation into the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework—the central agreement shaping how nations will tackle species loss. "They really are responsible for life on Earth," Mueller said of fungi, which number some 160,000 known species and serve as nature's recyclers, shuttling nutrients and water to plants, storing carbon in soil, and providing food for animals and people.

The oversight is staggering: most fungi lack any formal conservation status data, yet they silently sustain ecosystems worldwide. Co-leader Cátia Canteiro of Plantlife International posed the central challenge: "When we talk about halting extinction risk, how can we talk about it while ignoring a whole kingdom of life?" The new guidelines push for research on rare species, the integration of fungi into restoration efforts, and sustainable harvesting that benefits communities.

The strategy is already grounded in real-world success. In Uganda and Rwanda, mushroom cultivation generates household income while reducing pressure on wetlands home to threatened cranes. Women in Benin, which harbors 70 species of edible mushrooms, have built livelihoods through cultivation and sales. Scientists like Bernice Bancole from Benin are also revealing fungi's hidden potential: certain species act as natural pest controls against cereal borers that devastate crops like sorghum and maize. For the first time, fungi—long relegated to the shadows—are being recognized for what they've always been: essential architects of life itself.
quick_facts: First global fungal conservation strategy launched at UN biodiversity conference in Armenia
Scientists from 30 countries developed the integrated protection plan
Approximately 160,000 known fungal species currently lack formal conservation status
Mushroom cultivation in Uganda and Rwanda provides income and protects wetlands
Benin's 70 edible mushroom species support women's economic opportunities
